about: The words of the chain lost_brother (Data/encounters/chain_lost_brother_793.json; Design/content/chains/lost_brother.md): a brother and his son taken from the Frisian islands in 810 and sold, one south by the Rhine to the Verdun men, one east by Birka. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); nine news items; and an 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. Nothing here is quoted from any book: all of it is our own wording, the story of Imma (Bede IV.22) included. Nobody says 'slave trade' or 'Viking': they are the taken, a lot, a head, the Danes, the heathen men. Asulf (cast.asulf) names prices in ounces and never haggles twice. Holmfast (cast.holmfast) says the number first. The Frisians are dry. Liafbern, Wibern, Frethburg, Ingimar and Gundbert are invented. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Word from the islands
A man with a burned hand is asking along the landing for your house by name. He is off the islands. He was your brother's neighbour, and he has been walking for nine days.
Nobody counted them. The sea was ships from one sandbank to the other. We stood against them three times. After the third time there were not enough of us to stand, so we paid.
Liafbern was alive when they rowed him off. I saw that. He was sitting up and he was angry, and they do not carry off the ones who will not last.
The boy went in another ship. Wibern. He did not cry out. He was holding on to a sheep, and they took the sheep as well.

The king is on the Aller with the whole host, waiting for the Dane to come and fight. The Dane is dead. His own man killed him. And the great beast the Saracen king sent died at Lippeham. It has been that kind of summer.

There is a peace now. Twelve of ours and twelve of theirs swore it on the Eider. I have not heard that anybody's kin were in it. A hundred pounds of silver went north, and that is all that went either way.
Give him bread, a place by the fire and six pennies, and hear all of it
Ask the count's rider whether the king will buy the taken back
Thank him and say nothing more

He eats slowly, like a man who has taught himself to. The ships went home by the north, he says, heavy. What the Danes take alive they sell at the new market on the Slie, where their king set the merchants down. Then he sleeps where he sits.

The rider laughs, not unkindly. The king is building ships at every river mouth and has no penny over for people. 'If a man wants his kin, he goes and gets them. The Danes sell at Sliesthorp. They will sell to you as soon as to anyone.'

He nods, and goes on down the landing to find the next house on his list. He has eleven. You stand a while. Your brother's mound is by Doccinga, and somebody there will know more than a neighbour could see from a ditch.
The mound by the creek

The byre is black posts. The house stands, because it was raining. Your brother's wife is at the loom as if nothing else could be trusted to stay where it is put. The priest has walked over from the church with a wax tablet.
They did not want me. I was under the boat with the little ones and the Danes were in a hurry. I have thought about whether to be glad.
You will know him. The front tooth he broke on your father's oar. The white scar across the left hand from the eel spear. If they have cut his hair he will be in a worse temper than the tooth.
The boy has my band for a belt, red and undyed, the goose-foot pattern. Nobody else weaves it with the feet turned in. I did it wrong the first time and kept doing it.
Forty-three from these mounds. I am writing them all, because God knows them and I would like one other to. A list is a small thing. Kings have been moved by smaller.

In England once a taken man's bonds fell off him each morning. His brother, a priest, thought him dead and said Mass for him at that hour. In the end they sold him to a Frisian. We come into every story sooner or later.
Have the priest write down every name the islands lost, and carry the list
Take the silver the mound has dug up for the buying back, and give your word on it
Take only the end of the band she wove for the boy's belt, and promise nothing

It takes him until dark. Forty-three names in a small square hand, yours two among them, on a strip of calfskin he had been keeping for something better. He says there is nothing better. He will say the Mass for all of them, each morning, and see what falls off.

Frethburg lifts a hearthstone. Ninety pennies' weight in cut silver and old thin coin, some of it your mother's. Three neighbours watch you take it, which is what they came for. You say that you will bring them back. It sounds larger said aloud.

She cuts a hand's length from the end still on the loom and knots it so it will not run. 'Promise nothing,' she says. 'I have had promises. Show him that, and he will know I am alive, and that is as much as I can send.'
A man who remembers every sale

Asulf's pen is a fenced yard with a roof along one side and a trough. He feeds his lots; it is cheaper than burying them. He has a hazel switch in his hand and a row of notched sticks on a peg, one for each ship that sold to him this year.
The island lot. Nine ships sold to me. A man with a broken tooth who would not stand when he was told. A boy who came with a sheep. I do not forget stock. It would be bad for the trade.

I split it. Grown men go south: a Saxon walks them to the Rhine, and Franks from a town called Verdun buy there for Spain. The young go east. A Svea took the boy to Birka. Two roads. You have one boat.
The king who sent the ships is dead. His own man did it. I mention this so that you know there is nobody to complain to.
I have heard what was sworn on the Eider. I was not asked. Your two were sold out of the kingdom before any oath, so the king pays and I do not. That is a good oath. I could live under more like it.

He sells my people by the dozen and yours by the one, and he has never told a lie about either. The south road is the short one. The Verdun men do not keep a lot through a winter. They would have to feed it.
Lay a Frankish blade on his table for the whole telling and his own stick
Weigh him two ounces of silver for the telling and his stick
Carry water in his pen for a day, and listen

He bends the blade against his knee and lets it spring. Then he talks for as long as it takes to drink a horn. The Svea is Ingimar, with a farm behind the town at Birka. Asulf cuts you a stick with his mark and the price he was paid, and says he will send word east that the boy is asked for.

He weighs it himself, on his own scale, and gives back a clipping that was over. The Svea is Ingimar of Birka; the Franks buy at Mainz, in a yard by the Frisians' houses. He cuts a stick with his mark and the price he was paid. 'They know my mark. It saves talk.'

Forty buckets from the well to the trough. Nobody in the pen looks at you. At dusk Asulf tells you the two roads anyway, in as many words as there are roads. The Wend walks you to the gate and adds the names: Ingimar at Birka. A yard at Mainz, by the Frisians' houses.
Twelve and twelve

The town is full of horses. A day's ride west, on the Eider, twelve great men of the Franks and twelve of the Danes are to swear the peace the kings made over the winter. A Frankish clerk is buying fish and writing down what it cost. One of King Hemming's men is watching him write.

Count Wala leads ours. The king's own cousin. Theirs are led by two brothers of their king. Twenty-four great men, and I am the one who has to find them all dry fish in a town that sells mostly people.
A list? Written? Give it here. My count can do nothing with a man weeping on a riverbank. A list he can read out, and what is read out before twenty-four witnesses has to be answered.
You have kin who were taken. So has half that coast. My count cannot swear to a sorrow. If you had names, written, that would be another thing.
What was taken was sold. What was sold was sold again. A king can give back what is in his hand. This one is new, and his hand is not yet full.
Hemming wants the peace more than your king does. He has brothers. If somebody asked a thing that cost him little and looked like much, I would not say he would refuse it.
Give the clerk the list of names, and forty pennies to see it reaches his count
Ride to the Eider and say it yourself, in their tongue, before both twelves
Stand in the crowd and watch them swear

Three days later the clerk finds you on the jetty, pleased with himself. The count read the names out, all forty-three. A brother of the Danish king said that a king who keeps another king's farmers looks poor. It was sworn with the rest: those still in the kingdom go home by Lammas, and the price is made good for those sold out of it.

The list was read. The clerk says so twice. It was not sworn: there was the border to settle, and the winter had been long, and the great men wanted to go home. King Hemming's man cuts you a stick with his king's mark. 'Show the dealers this. It is not an oath. It is a king looking at them.'

You say it badly and they understand it. Forty-three farmers, by name, off islands that have paid their hundred pounds. Count Wala looks at you for some time. A brother of the Danish king laughs and says the Frisian has a point and a bad way of making it. It is sworn with the rest.

They swear on their weapons, the Danes and the Franks alike, on a wet meadow by a brown river. It takes less time than unloading a boat. The border is the Eider. Nobody says a word about anybody's kin, and by evening the horses are gone.
One who crossed himself
The road from Saxony comes down to the water here, and whatever walks it crosses in this man's boat. He counts everything he carries, because he is paid by the head, for oxen and for people alike.
Twelve on a rope and a Saxon with a stick. Three weeks back, or four. He paid for twelve Wends. I do not ask what a thing is. I ask how many.
When we pushed off, one of them crossed himself. Forehead, breast, shoulders, the way my mother does it. Wends do not. I noticed it, and then I had the current to mind.

They sell at Mainz, before the archbishop's steward. It has to be before somebody: that is the old king's law. If a man stood up there with a witness the steward knew, the Saxon's oath would not be worth the breath.
Pay him thirty pennies to come up the river and say it under oath
Ask him what else the road has brought down, and go on

He leaves the ferry to his son, who is pleased, and comes aboard with a loaf and a clean shirt for the oath. He has carried the archbishop's own oxen over this water for twenty years. 'The steward knows my face. He owes me for a calf.'

Oxen, he says, and Saxon horses, and fewer cloth boats than any year he remembers: the Frisians are late, and the Mainz men are paying over for a good cloak. He wishes you luck with your Wend. He says it as if he knows it is not a Wend.
Eleven Wends and a Frisian

A walled yard behind the Frisians' quarter. Twelve men sit along the wall with a rope through their belts. Eleven are Wends. The twelfth has a broken front tooth and a white scar across his left hand, and he has seen you and is being careful not to look.
Twenty-five shillings for that one. He is strong and he has all his fingers. In Saragossa they will give me three times that, and I have to walk him there and feed him. You see I am not a hard man.
The drover swore the whole rope heathen, on relics, before I paid. A Wend who has learned to make the cross is still a Wend. I have had them recite the whole Creed when they see the mountains.
You took your time. I have walked from one sea nearly to another, and I can tell you the middle of the world is mostly mud. Is the boy with you?
A lot is sold before me or it is not sold. Heathen men of the marches, yes. A free man of the king's own Frisians, no: the law of his country says who sells him out of it pays as for a killing.
My lord Riculf has ruled this church since before you had a beard. He does not like oaths sworn lightly in his court. He likes Verdun's merchants a little less.
My lord Haistulf is new in the chair and wishes to be known as careful. Bring me an oath I can stand behind, and he will be pleased with us both.
I know that ferryman. He has never lied to me about a head of cattle in twenty years, and he complains so much about what I owe him that he must be honest.
Buy him at the Verdun man's price
Swear him a free Frisian before the steward, with the ferryman's oath beside yours
Swear him a free Frisian with your crew as oath-helpers
Kneel to the steward and ask for the church's alms for the taken

Three hundred pennies, counted twice on a plank. Gundbert unties the rope himself and wishes you both health. Your brother says nothing until the gate is shut behind you. Then he says that he was worth more, and that he will pay it back, and that you are not to tell his wife the figure.

The ferryman swears to the cross made on the water. You swear to the tooth and the scar. Your brother says the Our Father in his own bad Latin and then, unasked, the names of your father's cows. The steward rules him free. The drover is gone, so the Verdun man pays the wrong, and pays it looking at you.

Your crew swear one after another that you are a man whose oath stands. Your brother says the Our Father, and then the names of your father's cows. The steward listens to the cows with more attention. He rules him free, and has the Verdun man weigh out the wrong. Gundbert weighs it slowly, so as to remember.

The steward asks which of your helpers knew this man before the raid. None did. The oath falls. He is sorry; he believes you; belief is not law. He buys your brother himself with the altar's silver, for the love of God, and writes your name in the church's book of what is owed.

You kneel on the stones of the yard in front of eleven Wends, your brother and a man from Verdun. The steward lets you stay there a moment longer than he need. Then he pays from the alms for the taken, and says the altar wants four cakes of wax within the year, and that he will know your boat.
An empty yard

The yard behind the Frisians' quarter has been swept. There is a ring in the wall and nothing tied to it. The archbishop's steward remembers the lot: it was sold before him, as the law asks, and nobody stood up to say a word.

Twelve heads, sworn heathen. One had a broken tooth and looked at me as if I should know better. I did not know better. Nobody was there to tell me. That is what the law is for, and that day it had nothing to work with.
Up the Mosel road to Verdun. From Verdun they go down the rivers to the south sea, and over the mountains to the Saracens. What a boat can follow ends here, at this wall.

I carry wine to Metz and Verdun every season and I know which houses buy men. For a pound of silver I will ask, and buy if he is there to buy. If he has gone over the mountains, you will have paid for an answer.
There are Masses at Saint Alban's for those who are away and cannot come back. The living are named in them. It costs a candle. I do not say it is the same as a rope cut.
Send a pound of silver after him with the carrier, and the marks to know him by
Ask for the archbishop's letter to the bishop of Verdun, and owe the church for it
Pay for a Mass at Saint Alban's, and turn the boat

The carrier ties the silver into his own belt and says the marks back to you: the tooth, the scar on the left hand, the temper. He goes at first light with six mules. 'After the vintage I come down again. Or he comes down without me. You will know at your own door, or you will not.'

The steward writes it himself, a hand's breadth of careful Latin, and seals it. One bishop greets another and asks after a free Frisian wrongly sold. It will go with the next clerk who rides west, which may be a month. 'A letter is slower than a rope of men. I tell you now so that you do not tell me later.'

You buy the candle. The priest at Saint Alban's asks the name, and writes it among the living, between a tanner's son gone to Rome and a woman nobody has seen since the flood. Then you go down to the boat. The river runs the right way for once.
The boy with the sheep

Holmfast walks you over the hill behind the town to a farm above the water. A boy is driving sheep off a boat's nets with a stick. He has grown a hand's width and his hair is cut the Svea way. He sees your cloak before he sees your face, and stops.
One boy. Frisian. Ten winters, now eleven. Bought at Sliesthorp by Ingimar for one mark less an ounce. I said I would show you the farm. I have shown it. That is one thing done.
He is a good boy. He does not steal and he is not sick. He talks to the sheep in his own tongue and they have started to listen. I would as soon keep him.
But kin is kin. A mark of silver, weighed. I paid less, and he has eaten since. Or wine: I have a daughter to marry and nothing in the house fit to pour.
He has a stick. I know the mark. The stick says a mark less an ounce and somebody's word behind it. Ingimar: the stick is the price. I say it twice. The stick is the price.
Is my father on the boat? No. Then where is he? You can tell me. I know how many they got for me.
Weigh out a mark of silver for him
Show the stick, and pay what he gave and no more
Give three casks of Rhine wine for him
Give your hand to carry his skins to Sliesthorp this summer for nothing

Holmfast holds the scale so that neither of you has to. A mark, level. Ingimar gives the boy the stick he herded with and tells him the sheep will miss him, which may be true. Then he asks what Frisian cloth costs where it is made, and orders six bolts for the wedding.

Ingimar turns the stick over, finds the mark, and breathes out through his nose. Seventy pennies' weight, and not a clipping more. He takes it well for a man who has just fed a boy a year for nothing. He orders six bolts of cloth, and you understand that the cloth will not be cheap.

He has the casks rolled up to the house before he says yes. He tastes one, counts them twice, and weighs you back forty pennies: nobody at his daughter's wedding is going to say he took a boy's price twice over. The boy carries the stick down to your boat and will not put it down.

You give your hand on it in front of Holmfast, who counts it as he counts everything. Eleven bales to Sliesthorp, unpaid, before the nights draw in. Your crew look at the bales and then at the sky. The boy gets into the boat without being told and starts to bail, though she is dry.
Gone with the summer ships

The farm above the water is shut and the boat shed is empty. Holmfast has the reckoning ready before you ask: the shipman went east after midsummer with four in the boat, and one of the four was a boy who bails.
Ingimar. One boat, four in it. Three men and a boy. East, after midsummer. You are late. I do not say it to wound. I say it because it is the first number.
He winters at Aldeigja and comes back with the skins when the ice goes. Or he goes on south from there with the ones who go south. Then the boy goes where the boat goes.
I go east myself at the next midsummer. A mark and a quarter: a mark for the boy, a quarter for me. If Ingimar will not sell, or the boy will not come, I keep the quarter. I say it now.
That is weaving. Goose feet, turned in. I will carry it for nothing. It weighs nothing. But a strip of wool does not buy a boy from a man who has taught him to steer.
Weigh Holmfast a mark and a quarter to buy the boy at Aldeigja and send him west
Send the end of his mother's band east, and let him choose
Ask Holmfast to say the boy is remembered, and turn the boat

He weighs it, says the weight, and has you say it back. A mark and a quarter, the boy Wibern, to be put on a westbound ship at Birka with food for the passage. 'A winter and a sea. Look for him at your own landing after the next harvest. If you do not see him, you will see me, with the mark.'

He winds the strip round two fingers and puts it inside his scale case, where he keeps nothing that is not silver. 'I will give it into his hand and say whose it is. After that it is his reckoning, not mine. He is eleven. At eleven I had been to Gotland twice.'

Holmfast repeats it: the boy Wibern is remembered at his mother's hearth. He will say it once, in Frisian if he can get his mouth round it. He does not say it is a small thing to carry, and you find that you are grateful.
Two at the table

There is a new byre on the mound, built of driftwood and one good oak post. Your brother is roofing it. The boy is handing him turves and speaking to the dog in the Svea tongue. Frethburg has set four bowls and is looking at them.
I set two bowls for a year. Then one day I set four, by mistake, and that was the day the boat came up the creek. I do not say it means anything. I shall go on setting four.
I know what a man costs now, which is more than most can say. I know what I cost and what the boy cost, and I am going to pay both, so do not start.
And the archbishop's wax. I was bought with altar silver like a candlestick. We will take him his four cakes, and a fifth so he cannot say Frisians count short.
That Verdun man will know your sail. He weighed that silver out like a man pulling his own teeth. I would stay off the Mosel wine for a year or two.
The Svear steer with the wind behind the ear and do not look at the land at all. I can show you. Ingimar said I had the hands for it. He said it to the sheep, but I was there.
One purse and two boats: take your brother as a sworn partner, and the boy to bail
Leave them the land; take the mound's weaving for the house, year on year
Take nothing: kin is not cargo

You swear it at the church door, hand on the post, the priest for witness: one purse, two boats, losses shared. The mound lays down its silver and twelve bolts of the red cloth. Your brother has walked across the world and says he would sooner sail the rest. The boy is in the bow before the cloth is stowed.

Your brother stays on his land, and nobody who has seen him roof that byre would move him. The mound's looms weave for your house first from now on, and Frethburg sets the price, which is fair and will stay fair. The boy is to come to you at fourteen. He has counted the years on his fingers twice.

You say it and mean it. In the morning there is silver under your rowing bench and ten bolts of cloth on top of it. Your brother is marking out ground beside his house with four pegs. 'A store. Yours. I am not asking.' He has his sea bag with him, and the boy has made himself one out of a sack.
The father's bowl
Your brother is mending a net on the bench by the door. He works as he always did, quickly and without looking. There is a small wooden bowl on the shelf above him that nobody has moved.
I am home. I say it each morning to see if it has become true. The byre is up. The eels are running. I have every thing I had before but one.

On a river in the east, with a Svea who feeds him and has taught him to steer. I have been a head on a rope. He is better off than I was. I tell myself that, and it is true, and it does no good at all.
Nobody can tell me where. East. That is a direction, not a place. I look at the sea in the mornings as if it might have an opinion.
Leave the bowl. He will be twelve at Martinmas, and then thirteen, wherever he is. I can count as well as any Svea.
One purse and two boats: take your brother as a sworn partner
Give him your hand on it: the summer the house sails east, he is in the boat
Leave him to his land; take the mound's weaving for the house

You swear it at the church door: one purse, two boats, losses shared. The mound lays down its silver and eight bolts of cloth. Your brother is a good hand in a boat and a silent one now. Whenever a ship comes in from the north he reads her crew, man by man, and then goes back to work.

He takes your hand and holds it too long. 'The summer you go. Not the summer after.' Frethburg cuts a new length of the goose-foot band and gives it to him, not to you. The silver and the cloth are in the boat already. It seems they were always going to be.

He will not leave the mound again, and says so before you ask. Frethburg's looms and her neighbours' weave for your house first from now on. Fourteen bolts go down to the boat. Your brother carries the last one himself and stands on the bank until the creek turns.
His father's knife

The boy is cutting reed on the creek bank with a knife too big for his hand. It was found in the ash of the byre. He has ground the burn off it himself. He does everything now as if somebody were about to tell him to stop.
It is his. I am keeping the edge on it. If he comes back and it is dull he will say I was badly brought up, and that would fall on him, so.
I am not a widow. The priest says so and the law says so. I have a husband in a country where they do not have winter. I have decided to think of him as warm.
Men have come back from the Saracens. I will not tell her how many years it took the ones I have heard of. She has not asked, and she is a woman who asks what she wants to know.

He is named at Saint Alban's among the living, I am told, and here each morning. If bonds can fall off in England they can fall off in Spain. I have not found the place where it is written that they cannot.
Take the boy into the boat and the house, before witnesses, as your own
Stand guardian of his father's share until he is a man, and build a store on it
Leave him with his mother; take the mound's weaving for the house

You set him on your knee before the neighbours, which is how it is done, and he is too big for it and bears it. The mound lays down silver and eight bolts of cloth for his keep. Frethburg ties his belt herself. In the boat he steers with the wind behind his ear and does not look at the land.

The neighbours witness it: his father's share is his, and yours to keep for him until he can carry a spear to the muster. You pace out a store by the creek. The boy paces it after you, checking. Silver and ten bolts of cloth go down to the boat as the first year's reckoning.

She needs him and he knows it, and that is the end of the talk. The looms of the mound weave for your house first from now on. Thirteen bolts go into the boat. The boy hands them down one at a time, and counts aloud, in two tongues.
The empty bench

The neighbours have come up the mound in their good cloaks. Nobody has died, so it is not a burial, and nobody knows what else to call it. The priest has the tablet with the names. Your brother's place on the bench has a folded cloak on it.
I wove that cloak for him while he was gone. It was something to do with my hands. Now it is done, and it fits a man who is not here, and I find I cannot cut it down for anyone else.
You took our silver and gave your word. I do not ask for the silver. I ask you to remember that there were three of us who heard you, and that we are still here.
The law does not know what to do with a man who is neither here nor dead. His share cannot lie idle. You are his brother. It comes to you, unless you say otherwise before these people.
The boy lives. Remember that when you choose. A Svea's boy on a far river is still his father's son, and might one day walk up this mound with a beard and ask whose store that is.
Take your brother's share of the mound, as the law gives it
Leave the land to Frethburg; take her weaving for the house
Give your share to Saint Boniface's church, for a Mass for the two of them every year

The neighbours witness it without a word, and it is yours: a strip of the mound, a share of the creek, room for a store. The kin count out what the land owes you in silver and cloth. Frethburg hands you the folded cloak with the rest. 'It goes with the share,' she says. It fits.

You say it before them all: the land stays where the loom is. Somebody's grandmother says 'well', which on this coast is a speech. Frethburg's cloth comes to your house first from now on. Fourteen bolts are in the boat by evening, and the cloak stays on the bench.

The priest writes it on the tablet under the forty-three names: a share of the mound to Saint Paul and Saint Boniface, and a Mass each year on the day of the raid. The neighbours bring cloth down to the boat, a bolt from one house, two from another, until you stop them. On every landing of this coast you will be the church's man now.
The boats from the Eider

There is smoke from every mound along the creek. The boats came at Lammas: thirty-one people of the forty-three on the priest's tablet, thin, and counted off the gunwale by a Dane with a tally stick. He is still here. He has a bag of weighed silver for the names that could not be found, and two of those names are yours.
Thirty-one. I read the names and they answered. I have said Mass for a good many years and never had the dead answer before. They were not dead, but I had begun to read them that way.

Thirty-one in the boats, and my two walked in by another road, because you fetched them. The Dane has silver for them all the same. Take it. Somebody should be paid for this year, and it had better be us.
Every mound on this creek got somebody back, and I have one of my two. I stood on the bank and counted the boats in with the rest. I was glad for them. I want that known, since I did not look it.
Thirty-one came up the creek and neither was mine. I baked for the ones who came. It is what there was to do. They ate it all.
Two names sold out of the kingdom before the oath. The king makes good the price, and the same again, because he is a new king. Whether you have found them since is not my reckoning.

The king heard how the names came to be read. He says a Frisian who can make twenty-four great men listen should sell his cloth at Sliesthorp and pay no man for the leave. I have his mark here, if you want it.
Take the silver for your two names, and the Danish king's peace for your boat at Sliesthorp
Take the silver, and your brother as a sworn partner in a second boat
Have the silver shared among the mounds that got nobody back
Take what is counted out for your two names, and nothing else

He counts the silver onto your thwart and cuts a stick with a mark you have seen once before, on the Eider. 'Show that at the jetty. You pay nothing there while this king lives, and I would not wager on the next.' The mounds send cloth down after him. The people of the creek have started calling you the one who speaks.

Your brother watches the Dane count the silver and says that it is the first time he has seen his own price paid in the right direction. You swear it at the church door: one purse, two boats. The islands have already decided who speaks for them at the count's court, and did not think to ask you.

The priest reads the twelve names that did not answer, and the silver is weighed out mound by mound. By evening there are sixteen bolts of cloth in your boat that you did not ask for, and the creek's whole people on the bank. When the count next wants a man to speak for the islands, they will send you.

You take the two prices and the cloth Frethburg presses on you, and leave the rest of the bag where it is. The Dane shrugs, and goes home on the ebb. But a thing done before twenty-four great men cannot be undone on a creek bank, and the islands call you their spokesman from that day.

Two hundred ships of the Danes were on the Frisian islands. The Frisians stood three times and then paid a hundred pounds of silver. People were carried off alive. The king is building ships and buying nobody back.
The peace is sworn on the Eider, twelve great men of the Franks and twelve of the Danes, on their weapons. The river is the border. Nothing was said of the people taken from the islands.

The peace is sworn on the Eider, and with it a new thing: the Danish king gives back the islands' people still in his kingdom by Lammas and pays the price of those sold out of it. A Frisian merchant brought the names.
A man of the islands and his son are home, one fetched from a Verdun merchant's rope at Mainz and one from a Svea's farm at Birka, by the same Frisian boat. Nobody on the coast has heard the like.
A Frisian taken from the islands is home, fetched off the road to Spain by his own brother. His son is still in the east with the Svear.
A boy taken from the islands is home from Birka, fetched by his father's brother. The father was sold south past Mainz and has not been heard of.
The mounds by Doccinga have held a day for those taken by the Danes and not come back. Forty-three names were read at Saint Boniface's church.
Boats came from the Eider at Lammas with thirty-one of the islands' people, given back under the peace, and silver for the rest. The mounds by Doccinga are smoking again.
The king has sent farmers home to the Frisians and paid for the ones he could not find. The dealers do not like it. A Frisian sells cloth on the jetty under the king's own mark.

A Frisian landing on a grey summer evening, the tide out: a thin man with a rag-bound burned hand stands asking at a boat's side; behind him a Frankish rider waters a tired horse; smoke far off over the flats.

A dwelling mound in the salt marsh under a wide white sky after rain: burned byre posts in front, a low turf house behind; in its doorway a woman at an upright loom with a red and white band on it; a tonsured priest in a seal-skin cloak writing on a wax tablet.

Sliesthorp, a wattle-fenced yard behind the booths at noon, autumn: people sitting under a lean-to roof by a water trough; in front a stout Dane with a plaited beard and a hazel switch, notched sticks hanging on a peg; a wide-faced Wend in a fur-edged cap at the gate.

A wet spring meadow by a brown river, low cloud: two lines of twelve cloaked men facing each other with swords and spears held upright, horses behind each line; in the crowd in front, a young Frankish clerk holding a strip of parchment.

The Rhine at the Ruhr's mouth on a windy afternoon: a broad flat ferry at a muddy landing where a rutted road comes down from the east; the ferryman, grey and thickset, leaning on his pole and making the sign of the cross to show what he saw.

Mainz, a walled yard in hard midday light: twelve men sitting along a wall with one rope through their belts; one has a broken front tooth and looks away; in front a well-dressed merchant with open hands and an older steward with keys and a staff.

The same yard at Mainz, empty and swept, late-autumn rain: an iron ring in the wall with nothing tied to it; the steward in the gateway under his hood; beyond the gate a carrier loading wine casks on mules.

A farm on a rocky hill above Birka's bay, bright early-summer morning, birches: a boy of eleven with cropped hair and a herding stick among sheep on spread fishing nets, a red and white woven belt at his waist; a spare Svea trader pointing; the farmer with folded arms.

The same farm above Birka, shut, on a still grey day at summer's end: a barred door, an empty boat shed with the rollers lying in the grass; the Svea trader holding a folding scale; far out on the water one small sail going east.

The mound at Doccinga on a clear evening: a new byre of driftwood, a man with a broken tooth on its roof laying turf, a boy handing turves up and a dog watching him; in the house doorway a woman with four wooden bowls.

The house door on the mound, low morning sun: a man mending a net on the bench without looking at his hands, his eyes on the sea; on a shelf above him one small wooden bowl; a woman in the dark of the doorway.
A creek bank below the mound, a windy bright day: a boy cutting reed with a man's knife too big for his hand; his mother on the slope above with a bundle of wool; the priest beside her looking south.

Inside the turf house, daylight from the door and the smoke hole: neighbours in their good cloaks standing along the walls; a bench with a folded new cloak on it and nobody sitting; the priest holding a wax tablet; a woman with her hands still.

The creek at Doccinga at high water on a warm Lammas evening: smoke rising from every mound to the horizon; two long Danish boats at the bank, thin people being helped ashore; a Dane with a tally stick and a leather bag in front, the priest reading from his tablet.
